The clause is enforceable (Section 3 below), and both lawyers already treat it that way — our letters invoked Exhibit C on October 25 and 27, and Ms. Lindqvist's own lawyer pointed you to it on September 29 ("We trust you have reviewed the parties' agreement in full"). Filing in court anyway would end in the same forum after a delay, at a fee cost that Exhibit C.3 may make yours to pay (Section 5). **Fees: Yes — if we prevail, and be clear-eyed that the clause is mutual.** Exhibit C.3: "The prevailing party in any arbitration or in any action to compel arbitration shall be entitled to recover its reasonable attorneys' fees and costs." If Pinecrest does not pay and we win in arbitration, we present a fee claim. The risk runs both directions: if we overreach — for example, on the conversion-fee count where implied-waiver exposure exists — they would seek their fees on that count. Fee discipline is not timidity; under a prevailing-party clause it is fee protection.

## 2. What the contract says — Exhibit C, verbatim

>
> **C.2** Class and consolidated proceedings are waived.
>
> **C.3** The prevailing party in any arbitration or in any action to compel arbitration shall be entitled to recover its reasonable attorneys' fees and costs.
>
> **C.4** Either party may seek provisional injunctive relief in court in aid of arbitration.
>
> **C.5** This Exhibit survives termination.
>
> **C.6** Notwithstanding Section C.1, claims solely for collection of undisputed invoices of less than $25,000 may be brought in small-claims court.

It also says the **arbitrability of any claim** goes to the arbitrator: a delegation clause, which is enforced if "clear and unmistakable" (*Rent-A-Center v. Jackson*, 561 U.S. 63 (2010), per `library/faa_2_4.md`) — and last-resort threshold objections by either side go to the arbitrator first, not to a judge.
- **C.2 (class waiver).** No effect on this matter either way; stated for completeness.
- **C.3 (fees).** The mutual prevailing-party clause — the subject of your fee question. It expressly reaches not only arbitration but **any action to compel arbitration**, which is exactly the scenario in Section 4.
- **C.4 (court carve-out that works for us).** The single way this dispute is heard in court: an injunction **in aid of** an arbitration, not instead of it. This is our C.4 tool against further uncompensated direct hires.

Lindqvist, Administrator" — and the election you are bound by is in an exhibit to the agreement you signed. Your October 6 questions were: (a) *"wants to 'hit them hard' in court,"* and (b) *"Can we at least make them pay our legal fees?"* Both were answered in substance in our October 25 demand and October 27 reply; you now get the full picture:

**Court: No — with one useful exception.** Exhibit C.1 of your signed agreement requires every dispute "arising out of or relating to this Agreement ... to be resolved **exclusively by binding arbitration**" administered by the American Arbitration Association (AAA) under its Commercial Arbitration Rules, before a single arbitrator seated in Capital City. Filing in court anyway would end in the same forum after a delay, at a fee cost that Exhibit C.3 may make yours to pay (Section 5). The one courtroom door that helps us is C.4: **provisional injunctive relief in court in aid of arbitration** — that is where the "stop them from hiring anyone else for free" motion lives.

**Fees: Yes — if we prevail, and be clear-eyed that the clause is mutual.** Exhibit C.3: "The prevailing party in any arbitration or in any action to compel arbitration shall be entitled to recover its reasonable attorneys' fees and costs." If Pinecrest does not pay and we win in arbitration, we present a fee claim. Fee discipline is not timidity; under a prevailing-party clause it is fee protection.

>
> **C.2** Class and consolidated proceedings are waived.
>
> **C.3** The prevailing party in any arbitration or in any action to compel arbitration shall be entitled to recover its reasonable attorneys' fees and costs.
>
> **C.4** Either party may seek provisional injunctive relief in court in aid of arbitration.
>
> **C.5** This Exhibit survives termination.
>
> **C.6** Notwithstanding Section C.1, claims solely for collection of undisputed invoices of less than $25,000 may be brought in small-claims court.

What each does for this case:

It also says the **arbitrability of any claim** goes to the arbitrator: a delegation clause, which is enforced if "clear and unmistakable" (*Rent-A-Center v. Jackson*, 561 U.S. 63 (2010), per `library/faa_2_4.md`) — and last-resort threshold objections by either side go to the arbitrator first, not to a judge.
- **C.2 (class waiver).** No effect on this matter either way; stated for completeness.
- **C.3 (fees).** The mutual prevailing-party clause — the subject of your fee question. It expressly reaches not only arbitration but **any action to compel arbitration**, which is exactly the scenario in Section 4.
- **C.4 (court carve-out that works for us).** The single way this dispute is heard in court: an injunction **in aid of** an arbitration, not instead of it. This is our C.4 tool against further uncompensated direct hires.
- **C.5 (survival).** The dispute clause survives termination — which takes the unknown §4 term/termination status almost entirely out of the forum analysis. (That unknown still matters for the §3 covenant's 12-month tail, and it remains on the open-items list.)
- **C.6 (small claims).** The literal reading is a double lock against us: (i) every invoice is over the cap, and (ii) J-4533 is disputed, so nothing would be "solely ... undisputed invoices" anyway. Smallest invoice is J-4571 at **$59,450.00** principal — **$60,539.92** including interest through October 25 ($59,450.00 + $1,089.92) — both far above $25,000. Courts stay suits on arbitrable issues (§3) and can compel arbitration (§4).

Filing in court anyway would end in the same forum after a delay, at a fee cost that Exhibit C.3 may make yours to pay (Section 5). If Pinecrest does not pay and we win in arbitration, we present a fee claim. The risk runs both directions: if we overreach — for example, on the conversion-fee count where implied-waiver exposure exists — they would seek their fees on that count. Fee discipline is not timidity; under a prevailing-party clause it is fee protection.

25: >
26: > **C.3** The prevailing party in any arbitration or in any action to compel arbitration shall be entitled to recover its reasonable attorneys' fees and costs.
27: >

It also says the **arbitrability of any claim** goes to the arbitrator: a delegation clause, which is enforced if "clear and unmistakable" (*Rent-A-Center v. Jackson*, 561 U.S. 63 (2010), per `library/faa_2_4.md`) — and last-resort threshold objections by either side go to the arbitrator first, not to a judge.
37: - **C.2 (class waiver).** No effect on this matter either way; stated for completeness.
38: - **C.3 (fees).** The mutual prevailing-party clause — the subject of your fee question. It expressly reaches not only arbitration but **any action to compel arbitration**, which is exactly the scenario in Section 4.
39: - **C.4 (court carve-out that works for us).** The single way this dispute is heard in court: an injunction **in aid of** an arbitration, not instead of it. This is our C.4 tool against further uncompensated direct hires.
